extracted.intended_audience: academics, program officers, and researchers interested in peer review and grant/fellowship panel deliberation (panelists and those who organize/evaluate panels)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative norms for academics serving on grant and fellowship review panels, describing what makes panel deliberation legitimate and what makes a 'good' or 'bad' panelist. Focuses on customary (informal) rules, interpersonal behavior, and strategic practices that shape funding decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparedness and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Show up fully prepared and ready to discuss the proposals; demonstrate a strong sense of responsibility and work ethic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preparedness and command of details enhance credibility and weight given to a panelist's opinion because they enable quick, thoughtful responses and better persuasion of others. Panelists who read carefully and offer thoughtful commentary are valued; lack of preparation undermines credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual breadth and expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate command of large literatures within one's field and have passive knowledge of several areas beyond it; be able to assess strengths and weaknesses across these areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists who read widely and retain knowledge are especially useful. Experts 'mark their territory' by staking claims to evaluate particular proposals based on past research or teaching, thereby legitimizing their judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succinctness and efficient use of time
rubrics_metrics.description: Be succinct in remarks; avoid wasting time with tangents, excessive detail, or unnecessary anecdotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels work at a fast pace with many proposals; verbose or long-winded speakers lose credibility and hinder collective decision-making. Chairs and effective panelists are brisk and efficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to communicate across disciplinary boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Articulate one's point of view so that those outside one's field can understand it; be accessible to nonexperts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This skill is especially prized on multidisciplinary panels, where cross-field intelligibility helps the group learn from one another and arrive at informed judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for others' expertise and sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Listen respectfully to co-panelists, be open to being convinced by others, and avoid unnecessarily confrontational or contemptuous behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respectful interpersonal interaction fosters trust and influence; rude, irreverent, or insensitive remarks erode credibility and can derail deliberation. Respect also includes being heard and having one’s contributions treated seriously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deferring to expertise / respecting disciplinary sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: Give greater weight to opinions of panelists whose expertise most closely overlaps the proposal's subject matter; accept disciplinary claims to evaluate certain work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deference is common and helps panels cope with unfamiliar topics; it can expedite decisions but may also limit discussion, suppress dissenting non-expert interventions, and create 'disciplinary intimidation' where non-experts defer rather than probe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collegiality and maintaining a respectful tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a consistently respectful, non-combative tone toward other panel members to keep deliberations functional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collegiality is seen as the 'oil' that keeps deliberation moving; it diffuses tension, enables compromise, and is taken as evidence of a 'well-functioning' panel even if it sometimes dampens vigorous debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bracketing personal interest and avoiding conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep personal connections, idiosyncratic preferences, and self-interest out of funding decisions; follow norms such as abstaining from votes involving one's students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal rules exist but are often weakly enforced; customary norms for abstention and bracketing promote legitimacy by reducing perceived partiality. Panelists are expected to avoid mobilizing networks to advantage applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to customary (informal) rules over formal guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on informal, learned rules of deliberation (customary rules) that standardize procedures and legitimize outcomes, rather than strictly following written program mandates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists often privilege ritualized, informal norms (deferring to expertise, collegiality, etc.). Formal guidelines may be consulted but are rarely strictly enforced; panels sometimes fund proposals that do not match formal competition focus if judged excellent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocity, consensus orientation, and equal opportunity to speak
rubrics_metrics.description: Strive for consensual decisions grounded in reasoned exchange, give full and equal voice to participants, and aim to realize the common good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The deliberative ideal (reciprocity/equality of voice) legitimates panels, though practical inequalities (expertise, prestige, demographics) limit perfect realization. Accountability is to the funding organization and the broader academic community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of alliances and personal/intellectual affinities
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists often form shifting alliances based on intellectual or theoretical affinities; these alignments influence evaluations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such affinities are not necessarily seen as corrupting; they are framed as use of one’s intellectual tools. Alliance formation is understood as case-by-case rather than permanent blocs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic voting norms (acceptable and illegitimate forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists may vote strategically (e.g., 'high-balling' to boost chances or to support someone they will defend), but deliberately assigning low ranks ('low-balling') to kill otherwise-strong proposals is widely regarded as illegitimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic voting is common and often tolerated as part of tactical negotiation, particularly late in deliberations. Low-balling is singled out as unfair because it effectively ends a proposal's chance of funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horse-trading and negotiation in final allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage in quid pro quo bargaining and negotiated trade-offs, especially in the final stages when choosing among similarly flawed proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horse-trading is treated as an ordinary, sometimes necessary aspect of parceling out scarce awards. Panelists weigh what they must concede to win other priorities and sometimes accept compromises for credibility or reciprocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional and interpersonal competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Possess interpersonal skills, appropriate presentation of self, moral character, and sensitivity to others; recognize evaluation as an emotional as well as cognitive process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviewees emphasize enjoyment, intellectual pleasure, and moral signaling as central; emotional labor and presentation affect perceived 'goodness' as a panelist and the legitimacy of deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority grounded in formal training and reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: A panelist's authority derives from formal technical training (PhD) and reputation; individual credibility affects their relative weight within the panel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although all panelists share formal legitimacy, reputational differences make some voices more influential. Panelists may explicitly cite their credentials or past research to claim evaluative authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-awareness and sensitivity to timing effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that timing of judgments affects evaluation dynamics (e.g., end-stage bargaining, last-available fellowships influence strategy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions and willingness to compromise shift over the course of a meeting; panelists should plan strategies accordingly and recognize that late-stage contexts encourage negotiation and strategic behavior.
